tldr: A new World Action Model that achieves both high speed and robustness against environmental shifts by explicitly predicting compact future hand motion, instead of generating heavy future videos at inference time.
hero_caption: Comparison between the proposed MoWAM and existing methods. It retains out-of-distribution robustness on par with Joint-WAM (yellow), which generates full future videos, while achieving near-instant inference speed (actions generated per second) close to Fast-WAM (blue), which skips future generation entirely.
overview:
World Action Models (WAMs) that incorporate future visual predictions have drawn significant attention for helping robots understand how their actions impact the environment. However, generating entire future video sequences during each inference step creates massive computational and memory overhead, making real-time control on physical robots practically impossible. On the other hand, completely discarding future video generation at inference to reduce compute leads to a sharp performance drop whenever the robot faces unseen environments or unexpected changes (out-of-distribution conditions).

To break this dilemma, the authors asked a fundamental question: "Does a robot really need high-fidelity future videos with backgrounds and textures just to decide its next move?" The essential information for robot control does not lie in the visual textures of the surroundings, but in motion: how the robot's own hand should move under interaction constraints with the environment. This insight led to MoWAM (Motion-based World Action Model).

During training, MoWAM learns rich physical dynamics through future video generation. At inference time, it completely removes video generation and explicitly predicts only lightweight "structured motion" represented by keypoints on the fingertips and palm. In experiments on simulation benchmarks (LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus) and real Franka arm manipulation tasks, MoWAM demonstrated out-of-distribution robustness comparable to full-video generation models while significantly reducing latency. Furthermore, because motion prediction is extremely lightweight, MoWAM easily enables "inference-time scaling"—sampling multiple candidate trajectories and selecting the best one with a verifier.
contributions: Proposed a new WAM paradigm that replaces heavy future video generation with lightweight, keypoint-based structured future motion prediction.

Constructed a dual-branch Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that learns visual dynamics via video generation during training, while decoupling video generation at inference to jointly predict actions and motion.
Introduced an inference-time scaling approach that uses predicted future motion to score and select the best candidate from multiple samples, further boosting task performance.

Demonstrated superior inference speed, out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, and higher task success rates over representative baselines in both simulation and real-world Franka manipulator experiments.

sections.heading: Why Predict Motion Instead of Future Video?
sections.summary: While WAMs that predict future visual changes are powerful, generating videos incurs prohibitive computational costs. Skipping video generation hurts robustness under distribution shifts, so this work adopts structured hand motion as a compact future representation.
sections.details:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly output robot control commands from vision and language have emerged as a foundation for generalist robot control. However, they lack explicit reasoning about how the world changes in response to their actions. To address this weakness, World Action Models (WAMs) have integrated the priors of video generative models.

Yet, existing WAMs face an acute trade-off during inference. Approaches that faithfully generate future video rollouts can accurately perceive situations even under novel objects or spatial shifts (distribution shifts), but the immense computational cost hinders real-time execution. Conversely, fast variants like Fast-WAM, which skip inference-time video generation and rely solely on observation features, leave future dynamics only implicitly encoded in latent features, making them brittle to environmental changes.

The authors recognized that the future information truly necessary for control is not the background texture, but the interaction itself: how the hand moves and how the gripper opens and closes. Instead of reconstructing the complete future scene, the proposed MoWAM explicitly predicts structured hand motion. This completely avoids the heavy overhead of video generation while preserving robust predictive capabilities under out-of-distribution changes.

sections.heading: The Evolution and Efficiency Bottlenecks of World Action Models
sections.summary: Prior works have explored joint generation of future videos and actions, as well as acceleration via distillation or latent dynamics. MoWAM sets itself apart by using interpretable, lightweight robot motion as an explicit future representation.
sections.details:
### II-A Trends in World Action Models
With the rapid rise of video foundation models, research integrating robot action prediction with future video generation has advanced quickly. Frameworks like UWM, DreamZero, and Motus use diffusion models to jointly generate video and actions in the same space, or condition actions on generated video rollouts, demonstrating impressive control performance. However, all these approaches require dense, high-resolution video rollouts at inference time, leading to severe execution delays.

### II-B Efforts toward Efficient WAM Inference
To mitigate this computational overhead, researchers have explored generative model distillation, coarse future representations, and asynchronous execution. More aggressive strategies completely remove full video generation at inference (such as Fast-WAM), model transitions purely within self-supervised latent spaces (JEPA-WAM), or predict only future subgoal images (LaWAM).

However, confining future information entirely to implicit features or latent spaces makes policies susceptible to performance drops when the environment drifts from the training distribution. MoWAM maintains the lightweight nature of video-free inference while using concrete, explicit geometric structures—robot body motion—as the future representation, offering a fresh way to resolve this trade-off.

sections.heading: MoWAM Architecture: How to Represent and Predict Lightweight Future Motion
sections.summary: The method defines geometric changes across three keypoints (fingertips and palm) as structured motion, combining a Video Transformer and an Action-Motion Transformer. Video generation is discarded during inference, producing only lightweight motion and actions.
sections.details:
### III-A Problem Formulation and Idea
Conventional WAMs generate future visual latents $\mathbf{v}$ from current observations and condition action prediction on them. Fast-WAM eliminates the explicit generation of $\mathbf{v}$ to output actions directly from observation features, but this harms robustness under distribution shifts. MoWAM replaces the heavy future video $\mathbf{v}$ by jointly modeling future robot motion $\mathbf{m}_{1:H}$ and actions $\mathbf{a}_{1:H}$ via the formulation $p_\phi(\mathbf{a}_{1:H}, \mathbf{m}_{1:H} \mid \mathbf{o}, \ell)$.

### III-B Structured Motion Representation
The key lies in how future motion is compactly represented. The method projects three keypoints—the left and right fingertips and the palm—onto the image plane, computing three geometric quantities: the gripper center position, the finger span, and the relative offset from the palm. The inter-step displacement of these quantities forms the temporal dynamics component $\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{dyn}}$, while the instantaneous relative configuration forms the structural component $\mathbf{m}_{\mathrm{str}}$. Crucially, this predicts how the hand will actually evolve under current scene constraints, rather than simply projecting open-loop control commands.

### III-C Architecture, Training, and Inference Flow
MoWAM adopts a dual-branch Mixture-of-Transformer architecture consisting of a Video Transformer and an Action-Motion Transformer. During training, the Video branch learns rich physical dynamics through future video denoising (Flow Matching), while the Action-Motion branch jointly learns actions and motion by attending to observation Key/Value features from the Video branch.
The inference design is particularly clever: the Video branch only runs a single forward pass on the current observation frame to extract features, bypassing the future video frame generation loop entirely. Sampling actions and motion from random noise using only the Action-Motion branch results in exceptionally fast execution.

### III-D Motion-Aware Inference-Time Scaling
Because generating future motion is computationally negligible, multiple candidate action-motion pairs can be sampled simultaneously at inference time. The authors train a task-progress verifier using ranking loss on successful human demonstrations alongside perturbed trajectories (spatial shifts and early cutoffs). During inference, the policy selects and executes the candidate with the highest verifier score, effectively using extra test-time compute to drive up task success rates.

captions.F2: Overall framework of MoWAM. The Action-Motion Transformer on the left jointly predicts actions and hand motion, while the Video Transformer on the right supplies observation features. Future video generation (bottom-right purple box) is only executed during training; at inference, video generation is completely detached.

sections.heading: Empirical Speed and Robustness in Simulation and on Real Robots
sections.summary: Evaluated on LIBERO, the out-of-distribution benchmark LIBERO-Plus, and a physical Franka robot. MoWAM matches the robustness of full-video generation models while slashing latency by a large factor, and demonstrates clear gains through inference-time scaling.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Simulation experiments were conducted on standard LIBERO (4 suites, 40 tasks in total) and LIBERO-Plus, which features 7 types of out-of-distribution variations including lighting, camera viewpoints, backgrounds, and object perturbations. Real-world experiments used a Franka Research 3 arm across three tasks: "Pick Banana", "Stack Bowls", and "Close Drawer" (100 demonstrations each, evaluated over 20 trials per task). Wan2.2-5B served as the backbone, and latency was measured on an RTX 5090 GPU.

### IV-B Main Results: High Success Rates and Rapid Inference
- **LIBERO (In-Distribution)**: MoWAM achieved an average success rate of 98.9%, outperforming Fast-WAM (96.5%) by 2.4 points and matching large models that generate complete future videos.
- **LIBERO-Plus (Out-of-Distribution / OOD)**: The advantage of explicit future prediction stood out clearly here. MoWAM achieved an average success rate of 81.43%, leading Fast-WAM (70.43%) by 11.0 points. While approaching the robustness of full-video generation models like Joint-WAM (86.29%) and IDM-WAM (85.86%), its action generation latency was only 293.5 ms—less than one-third of Joint-WAM (766.3 ms) and IDM-WAM (995.4 ms).
- **Real-World Experiments**: MoWAM attained an 80% average success rate, outperforming Fast-WAM (45%) by 35 points. Compared to Motus, which generates video rollouts (70% average success, 1621.9 ms latency), MoWAM achieved higher success while cutting latency to under one-fifth.

### IV-C Inference-Time Scaling and Ablations
- **Inference-Time Scaling**: On the physical "Pick Banana" task, increasing the number of candidates $K$ from 1 to 4 and 8 steadily improved success rates from 65% to 75% and 80%. Video-generating baselines face memory explosions (OOM at $K=32$) and latency spikes, whereas MoWAM can sample 8 candidates in less time than a video baseline takes to generate a single candidate.
- **Importance of Training-Time Video Modeling**: Freezing the Video DiT and using only pretrained features caused the success rate to plummet from 76.0% to 33.1%, confirming that predicting video during training is essential for instilling physical world dynamics.
- **Motion Prediction Accuracy**: Comparing MoWAM's predicted motion against open-loop projected actions (Action-Proj.) showed a 92.75% reduction in pixel-space average displacement error (ADE), dropping from 77.56 down to 5.63. This confirms the model accurately predicts physical interactions and constraints with the environment.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Explicit Future Motion Opens Up Practical Robot Foundation Models
sections.summary: MoWAM removes the burden of video generation while explicitly predicting future motion, achieving both high speed and out-of-distribution robustness. It also provides a viable path for inference-time scaling by spending compute during testing.
sections.details:
MoWAM reconciles two goals that were previously difficult to balance: physical world understanding via world models and the computational efficiency needed for real-time control. Its design is thoroughly pragmatic—absorbing environmental dynamics through video generation during training, while discarding unnecessary background synthesis during inference to focus entirely on hand motion.

Furthermore, its ability to support inference-time scaling—scoring predicted motions with a verifier to pick the best action candidate within practical latency and memory budgets—provides a powerful tool for operating robot foundation models. Rather than predicting every detail at the pixel level, this work underscores the profound importance of choosing the right task- and embodiment-level abstraction.

takeaways: The future information needed for robot decision-making can be effectively represented by structured hand motion rather than entire scene videos.
Supervising video prediction during training remains crucial, as it grounds the model in the physical laws and dynamics of the real world.
Adopting a lightweight future representation makes inference-time scaling—generating and verifying multiple action candidates—practical under realistic time and memory limits.
limitations: Relying on three hand keypoints means generalizing to deformable objects, multi-fingered hands, or tasks with complex multi-point contacts may require additional design considerations.

Under severe camera perspective shifts (such as heavy occlusions or large viewpoint offsets), 2D keypoint projections may recover less geometric information than full 3D voxel or point cloud representations.
Under extreme initial state or camera viewpoint perturbations in OOD benchmarks, MoWAM still trails full-video generation models by a few percentage points.
